name: Total THC standard
where_it_stands: Federal hemp law is switching from a delta-9 THC test to a total-THC test that counts THCA and other THC forms, with a 0.4 mg per-container cap on finished products. That switch takes effect on 11 December 2026 after a one-month delay.

next_milestone.text: Total-THC definition of hemp and 0.4 mg per-container cap take effect for products, unless Congress acts.

summary: Under the 2018 Farm Bill, hemp meant cannabis with no more than 0.3% delta-9 THC by dry weight, which allowed products high in THCA, delta-8 and other THC forms. USDA's 2021 hemp production rule already required growers' crops to be tested for total THC, but the statutory product definition still turned on delta-9. Public Law 119-37 changes the statute itself: hemp must have no more than 0.3% total THC including THCA, intermediate products are capped at 0.3% total THC and similar cannabinoids, and finished products at 0.4 milligrams per container. Most of this now applies from 11 December 2026.

what_changes.text: THCA flower and pre-rolls that pass a delta-9 test but exceed 0.3% total THC stop being hemp, and finished goods must fit under 0.4 mg per container.
THCA flower and most hemp THC edibles and drinks will no longer be federally lawful hemp after 11 December 2026.
Testing labs and compliance costs shift; the House-passed 2026 farm bill would also write total-THC testing for crops into the hemp production statute.

timeline.event: 2018 Farm Bill sets the 0.3% delta-9 THC definition of hemp
USDA final hemp production rule requires total THC testing of crops (effective 22 March 2021)
Public Law 119-37 rewrites the hemp definition around total THC including THCA
House passes the 2026 farm bill (H.R. 7567), which would codify total-THC testing for hemp crops
Total-THC hemp definition takes effect after the September delay

faq.a: It counts all tetrahydrocannabinols in a product, including THCA, which turns into delta-9 THC when heated, rather than delta-9 THC alone.

Until 11 December 2026 federal law still uses the delta-9 test for products. After that, flower above 0.3% total THC including THCA is no longer hemp under federal law. State laws may already be stricter.

faq.q: How much THC can a hemp product contain under the new rule?
faq.a: No more than 0.4 milligrams of total THC, including similar cannabinoids, per container.
